summary: Dr. Claw is an AGPL-3.0 research workspace that wraps existing command-line coding agents (Codex and Claude SDKs) with a task graph, an artifact store, a decision log, an execution trace, permission policies and a skill library of 171 skills (58 mapped to research stages). The automated evaluation runs three medical ML tasks (two Derm7pt classification problems and a clinical-note risk baseline) once each, with Codex/gpt-5.4 inside versus outside the workspace under the same permissions. Completeness, the fraction of 21 author-chosen best-practice elements present in the output files, is 0.952 versus 0.873, with a bootstrap CI of [-0.00, +0.14]. There is also one induced-failure recovery demo and a retrospective human study with seven AI PhD students. The domain is AI-for-science research workflows, not software development teams.

claims.claim: Holding the executor fixed, Dr. Claw scores higher on research completeness than the bare agent it wraps
claims.evidence: Pooled 0.952 vs 0.873 over three tasks with one run each; the 95% bootstrap CI [-0.00, +0.14] includes zero (§5.1). Modeling elements pass at 1.00 in both conditions. The whole gap comes from three hygiene elements (limitations section, subgroup analysis, real citations) that the bundled reference-audit and paper-writing skills are written to add. The 21-element rubric was chosen by the authors. Scoring is deterministic, but it checks presence, not correctness (acknowledged).

claims.claim: Dr. Claw turns a flat pile of files into an auditable, recoverable process trail
claims.evidence: Every run persists a task graph (mean 14 nodes), an execution trace (14 transitions) and a decision log (10 entries); the bare agent persists none. The authors concede this holds by construction because these objects are Dr. Claw's own file format. On a format-neutral check, write-up file references resolve at 100% vs 62%, but on 48 vs 8 references, which the authors call volume-confounded and non-decisive.

claims.claim: The workspace recovers from step failures non-destructively, preserving prior state
claims.evidence: A single induced wrong-path error in one Derm7pt mini-project, recovered to accuracy 0.892 with 5 prior files retained. The authors state there is no matched bare-agent recovery run.

claims.claim: Operators using Dr. Claw finish faster, produce higher-rated output, switch tools less and report better experience
claims.evidence: Seven AI PhD participants who had a three-week free-use period with Dr. Claw only. Dr. Claw sessions were live-logged, while both control conditions were reported from recall. Friedman tests are significant, but most Holm-corrected pairwise p-values are 0.047-0.125, the smallest attainable at n=7. Time is reported in coarse bands. The authors label it exploratory, not causal.

patterns.note: A versioned, schema-checked SKILL.md library is attached to task nodes by a stage-skill map. Invocation is only suggested in the prompt and is not enforced; the one reference audit that did not fire explains the tied task. The skills are not ablated separately from the rest of the bundle.
A task graph with dependencies, status and next-action prompts drives execution. No comparison isolates the graph from the skills.
A persistent pipeline-state store, artifact store and decision log carry state across sessions.
A timestamped execution trace and decision log are persisted per run. Their oversight value is asserted, not measured.
Human approval checkpoints are part of the design, but the automated comparison ran under an approval-never profile, so the gate was never exercised in the evaluation.
Allow/deny permission checks with denial reasons and bounded approval timeouts. Not evaluated.
Claim-to-evidence maps link write-up claims to produced files. The only check (100% vs 62% resolving references) is volume-confounded and not about requirements or code.

methodology.sample: Three open-ended medical ML research tasks, one run per condition; one induced-failure demo; seven participants in the human study
methodology.baselines: Bare Codex CLI with the same model and the same danger-full-access/approval-never profile. No other orchestration framework and no skill-only or graph-only variant.
methodology.models: gpt-5.4 via the Codex provider only
methodology.variance: Bootstrap CI over three task-level deltas from single runs; no repeated runs. Human study: Friedman and Holm-corrected Wilcoxon on n=7.
methodology.ablations: None; the task graph, state objects, skills and workflow instructions are evaluated as one bundle (acknowledged)
methodology.contamination_controls: n/a; the rubric was not shown to either condition
methodology.languages: Not reported; generated research code in an ML stack, presumably Python

standards.artifacts: GitHub OpenLAIR/dr-claw under AGPL-3.0; the medical datasets stay on the authors' server and are not redistributed

biases.detail: The authors define the 21 completeness elements, and their own bundled skills target exactly the three elements where the conditions differ.
Completeness counts whether elements are present, not whether they are correct or scientifically sound (acknowledged).
Three tasks with one run each, one recovery demo, and seven participants.
No repeated runs per task; the bootstrap is over three task deltas and its CI includes zero.
AI PhD participants got three weeks of free use with Dr. Claw only. The controls were recalled retrospectively while Dr. Claw sessions were live-logged.
Only gpt-5.4 through the Codex provider is evaluated, although the system claims compatibility with several executors.
The Table 1 design-space comparison against other research-agent systems is marked from papers, documentation and repositories, not from runs of those systems.
The paper says Dr. Claw 'remains slower' but does not quantify the time or token overhead.

coi.affiliations: Lehigh University, University of Illinois Chicago, University of Pennsylvania, University of Maryland, University of Notre Dame, University of British Columbia
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: The authors' own open-source system wrapping third-party agent CLIs
coi.detail: Academic authors evaluating their own released system with their own rubric. No vendor tie.

verdict_reason: The headline completeness gain rests on three tasks with one run each and a CI that includes zero. The gain comes entirely from elements the system's own skills are written to add. The auditability result is true by construction, the recovery result is a single demo without a control, and the human study compares live logs against recall for seven pre-familiarized participants. The paper is candid about all of this, but there is no admissible evidence left, and the domain is AI-assisted scientific research rather than software teams.
applicability: Little transfers to the Java multi-repo team. The one usable idea is that a persisted decision log plus task graph could serve as a handoff artifact between mixed agent hosts, since state lives in files rather than in a chat transcript. That is untested here. The paper's own triggering finding is the more useful warning: placing a skill suggestion in the prompt did not guarantee the skill ran, and the one non-firing audit erased the gain on that task. If the team relies on skills for spec or onboarding checks, verify from the trace that they executed instead of trusting the prompt.
